title: Food chains & webs
group: BIO-EVOL / BIO-ECOL / BIO-PLANT — Evolution, Ecology & Plants
examples: What is the difference between a food chain and a food web?
If all the producers disappear, what happens to the consumers?
Can you give an example of a decomposer in a forest?

explain.say: Today we will learn about how energy moves in nature. We will look at food chains and food webs.

items: Consumers eat other things for energy

explain.say: Producers are organisms that make their own food using sunlight. Plants are the most common type of producer.
Consumers are organisms that must eat other things to get energy. Animals are usually consumers in these chains.
A food chain shows a single path of energy transfer. Grass eaten by a rabbit is a simple example.
A food web shows many interconnected food chains. This shows how complex life is together. Think of it like a big net.
If we remove a key species, like a main predator, the whole web can change greatly. This shows the balance of nature.

draw.text: Removing species affects the whole web

faq.q: What is the difference between a food chain and a food web?
faq.a: A food chain shows one single path of energy flow. A food web shows many interconnected food chains together.
asks: How do I know which one to draw?

faq.q: Do decomposers count as producers or consumers?
faq.a: Decomposers break down dead matter. They are important because they recycle nutrients back into the soil for producers.

faq.q: What happens if all the producers die?
faq.a: If producers die, the herbivores that eat them will soon run out of food. This affects the carnivores that eat the herbivores too.
asks: What is the first thing to suffer?

faq.q: Can an animal be both a consumer and a producer?
faq.a: Some animals, like bears, can eat berries and also eat meat. This means they can be both types of feeders.
asks: Can one animal fit both roles?

faq.q: Is energy lost when it moves up the food chain?
faq.a: Yes, energy is lost at each level. Only about ten percent of the energy moves to the next level up.

facts: Producers, like plants, create their own food using photosynthesis.
Herbivores are consumers that only eat producers.
Carnivores are consumers that eat other animals.
Decomposers break down dead organisms, recycling nutrients.

quiz.why: The bird eats the grasshopper, making it a secondary consumer in this chain.

wrong.0: This is the organism that makes its own food, which is the grass.
wrong.1: There is no organism shown that eats the bird in this simple chain.
wrong.3: This is the level that eats the producer, which is the grasshopper.

quiz.say: A bear eating berries and fish is best described as:
quiz.why: An omnivore eats both plants and animals, like the bear doing.

wrong.1: This only describes eating plants, like the berries.
wrong.2: This only describes eating meat, like the fish.
wrong.3: This describes making food from sunlight, which the bear cannot do.

quiz.say: If decomposers were removed from an ecosystem, what would happen?

options.show: The energy flow would stop completely.
options.say: The energy flow would stop completely.

options.show: Nutrients would build up and not be recycled.
options.say: Nutrients would build up and not be recycled.

quiz.why: Decomposers break down dead things, releasing nutrients back for producers to use again.

wrong.0: The entire system relies on nutrient cycling, affecting all levels.
wrong.1: Energy still flows, but the recycling of matter, which is crucial, would halt.
wrong.3: While it would be bad, the death is not instant; recycling is the main issue.
